prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In line with the local philicity concept proposed by Chattaraj et al. (Chattaraj, P. K.; Maiti, B.; Sarkar, U. J. Phys. Chem. A. 2003, 107, 4973) and a dual descriptor derived by Toro-Labbe and coworkers (Morell, C.; Grand, A.; Toro-Labbe, A. J. Phys. Chem. A. 2005, 109, 205), we propose a multiphilic descriptor. It is defined as the difference between nucleophilic (Wk+) and electrophilic (Wk-) condensed philicity functions. This descriptor is capable of simultaneously explaining the nucleophilicity and electrophilicity of the given atomic sites in the molecule. Variation of these quantities along the path of a soft reaction is also analyzed. Predictive ability of this descriptor has been successfully tested on the selected systems and reactions. Corresponding force profiles are also analyzed in some representative cases. Also, to study the intra- and intermolecular reactivities another related descriptor namely, the nucleophilicity excess (DelW-+) for a nucleophile, over the electrophilicity in it has been defined and tested on all-metal aromatic compounds.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Chattaraj, Maiti, Sarkar

outputs.L1: Building on the local philicity concept proposed by Chattaraj et al. (Chattaraj, P. K.; Maiti, B.; Sarkar, U. *J. Phys. Chem. A* 2003, 107, 4973) and the dual descriptor developed by Toro-Labbe and coworkers (Morell, C.; Grand, A.; Toro-Labbe, A. *J. Phys. Chem. A* 2005, 109, 205), we propose a multiphilic descriptor defined as the difference between the nucleophilic (Wk+) and electrophilic (Wk−) condensed philicity functions. This descriptor can simultaneously account for the nucleophilicity and electrophilicity of specific atomic sites within a molecule. Variations in these quantities along the pathway of a soft reaction are also examined. The predictive capability of the descriptor has been successfully tested using selected systems and reactions, and the corresponding force profiles are analyzed for several representative cases. In addition, to investigate intra- and intermolecular reactivity, a related descriptor—namely, the nucleophilicity excess (DelW−+) of a nucleophile over its electrophilicity—has been defined and tested on all-metal aromatic compounds.
outputs.L2: Building on the local philicity framework introduced by Chattaraj and colleagues (Chattaraj, P. K.; Maiti, B.; Sarkar, U. J. Phys. Chem. A 2003, 107, 4973) and the dual descriptor developed by Toro-Labbe’s group (Morell, C.; Grand, A.; Toro-Labbe, A. J. Phys. Chem. A 2005, 109, 205), we introduce a multiphilic descriptor. This quantity is calculated by subtracting the condensed electrophilic philicity function (\(W_k^-\)) from the condensed nucleophilic philicity function (\(W_k^+\)). It therefore characterizes both the nucleophilic and electrophilic behavior of individual atomic sites within a molecule at the same time. Changes in these quantities along the course of a soft reaction are also examined. Tests involving selected chemical systems and reactions successfully demonstrate the descriptor’s predictive capability, while the associated force profiles are evaluated for several representative examples. In addition, a related parameter termed nucleophilicity excess (\(\Delta W^{-+}\))—which expresses the extent to which nucleophilicity exceeds electrophilicity in a nucleophile—is defined for investigating intra- and intermolecular reactivity and is tested on all-metal aromatic compounds.
outputs.L3:
A multiphilic descriptor is proposed by combining the concepts of local philicity and the dual descriptor within a unified framework. Defined as the difference between the condensed nucleophilic \((W_k^{+})\) and electrophilic \((W_k^{-})\) philicity functions at an atomic site \(k\), this quantity provides a simultaneous measure of the site’s tendency to participate in nucleophilic and electrophilic interactions. Its sign and magnitude therefore help identify the dominant reactivity character of each atom and distinguish among competing reactive sites within the same molecule.

The behavior of this descriptor is examined along selected soft-reaction pathways to determine how local reactivity evolves as reactants approach products. Its predictive performance is assessed for representative molecular systems and chemical reactions, together with the corresponding force profiles, thereby connecting changes in electronic reactivity with the mechanical progression of a reaction.

A complementary nucleophilicity-excess descriptor, denoted \(\Delta W^{-+}\), is also introduced. This descriptor quantifies the extent to which nucleophilic character exceeds electrophilic character and can be applied to both intramolecular and intermolecular reactivity. Its usefulness is evaluated using all-metal aromatic compounds, demonstrating its potential for identifying preferred reactive sites and interpreting the unusual reactivity patterns of these systems.
outputs.L4:
Within conceptual density-functional theory, local reactivity is commonly described using condensed nucleophilic and electrophilic philicity functions. To combine these complementary quantities into a single measure, a multiphilic descriptor is introduced for each atomic site \(k\), defined as

\[
\Delta W_k = W_k^{+}-W_k^{-},
\]

where \(W_k^{+}\) and \(W_k^{-}\) denote the condensed nucleophilic and electrophilic philicity functions, respectively. The sign and magnitude of \(\Delta W_k\) provide a direct indication of the dominant character of a site: positive values identify sites that are preferentially susceptible to nucleophilic attack, whereas negative values indicate sites more favorable for electrophilic attack. Values close to zero reflect a balance between the two tendencies. Because both types of reactivity are represented on a common scale, the descriptor can be used not only to rank atomic sites in an isolated molecule but also to monitor changes in their character along a soft-reaction pathway.

A related quantity, the nucleophilicity-excess descriptor \(\Delta W^{-+}\), is formulated to compare the nucleophilic contribution of one reacting center with the electrophilic contribution of another. This comparison makes the descriptor useful for analyzing both intramolecular and intermolecular processes. It can identify the most likely donor–acceptor pairing, reveal the direction of charge transfer, and distinguish between competing reactive sites without requiring separate and potentially ambiguous interpretations of several local indices.

The performance of these descriptors is examined for a representative set of chemical reactions and for selected all-metal aromatic compounds, in which unusual electronic delocalization can make conventional reactivity assignments difficult. The descriptors correctly identify the preferred nucleophilic and electrophilic centers and reproduce changes in local reactivity as bonds are formed or broken. Their evolution along the reaction coordinate is further interpreted through reaction-force profiles, which divide a reaction into regions associated with structural preparation, electronic reorganization, transition-state crossing, and product relaxation.

The combined analysis shows that the multiphilic and nucleophilicity-excess descriptors do more than predict the most reactive atomic sites. They also provide a unified explanation of how nucleophilic and electrophilic behavior develops during a reaction. Consequently, these quantities offer a compact and broadly applicable framework for describing site selectivity, charge-transfer direction, and the changing electronic character of reacting centers in both conventional molecular systems and compounds with nonclassical bonding or aromaticity.
outputs.L5:
Chattaraj, Maiti, and Sarkar are names associated with diverse contributions across education, research, culture, and public life in South Asia. Each surname carries a rich regional heritage, particularly within Bengal, while also reflecting the wider movement of people and ideas across the world.

Whether connected through academic collaboration, professional work, or a shared community, Chattaraj, Maiti, and Sarkar represent the value of combining different perspectives. Their collective presence can symbolize cooperation, intellectual exchange, and a commitment to progress. By sharing knowledge and experience, individuals bearing these names continue to contribute to their respective fields and inspire future generations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a computational chemistry paper introducing a “multiphilic descriptor” based on the difference between condensed nucleophilic and electrophilic philicity functions, citing Chattaraj et al. and Morell, Grand, and Toro-Labbe.
counterfactuals.output:
We introduce a local “multiphilic descriptor” for predicting site selectivity in chemical reactions, defined as the difference between the condensed electrophilic and nucleophilic philicity functions at atom \(k\),
\[
\Delta\omega_k=\omega_k^{+}-\omega_k^{-}
=\omega\left(f_k^{+}-f_k^{-}\right),
\]
where \(\omega\) is the global electrophilicity index and \(f_k^{+}\) and \(f_k^{-}\) are the condensed Fukui functions for nucleophilic and electrophilic attack, respectively. The formulation combines the local philicity concept developed by Chattaraj and co-workers with the dual-descriptor framework introduced by Morell, Grand, and Toro-Labbé. Because both reactivity channels are evaluated on a common energetic scale, \(\Delta\omega_k\) provides a compact measure of the dominant local character of an atomic site: positive values indicate preferential electrophilic character and susceptibility toward nucleophilic attack, whereas negative values identify nucleophilic sites favored for electrophilic attack. Values near zero signal ambiphilic or weakly differentiated centers. Computational applications to representative organic molecules demonstrate that the descriptor reproduces established regioselectivity trends while offering clearer discrimination than either condensed Fukui functions or individual philicity functions considered separately. The multiphilic descriptor therefore provides a simple, physically motivated tool for analyzing competing reactive tendencies and rationalizing site selectivity within conceptual density functional theory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that proposes a local reactivity descriptor capable of simultaneously identifying nucleophilic and electrophilic atomic sites, analyzes its variation along soft reaction pathways and force profiles, and applies nucleophilicity excess to all-metal aromatic compounds.
counterfactuals.output:
The study develops a conceptual-density-functional-theory descriptor that combines the two Fukui functions into a single local quantity, commonly written as the **dual descriptor**

\[
\Delta f(\mathbf r)=f^{+}(\mathbf r)-f^{-}(\mathbf r).
\]

Its sign distinguishes opposite kinds of reactive regions: positive values indicate electron-deficient sites susceptible to nucleophilic attack, whereas negative values indicate electron-rich sites susceptible to electrophilic attack. Thus, unlike separate Fukui-function maps, it identifies nucleophilic and electrophilic sites simultaneously and reduces ambiguities when both functions are large at the same atom.

The authors then follow this descriptor along low-energy, or “soft,” reaction pathways and compare its evolution with reaction-force profiles. Changes in local reactivity are shown to track the redistribution of electron density during the different stages of bond breaking, electronic reorganization, and bond formation, providing information complementary to energetic reaction coordinates.

Finally, the work uses a condensed form—expressed as **nucleophilicity excess**, the balance between nucleophilic and electrophilic Fukui responses at an atom—to study all-metal aromatic clusters. The analysis reveals how aromatic delocalization redistributes local reactivity among metal centers and helps identify which atoms or regions are most likely to participate in electrophilic or nucleophilic processes. Overall, the study presents the dual descriptor and nucleophilicity excess as compact tools linking local selectivity, reaction progress, and aromatic electron delocalization.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a journal-style abstract defining the multiphilic descriptor as the difference between \(W_k^+\) and \(W_k^-\), explaining its predictive applications to chemical reactions and its relationship to local philicity and the dual descriptor.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**—The multiphilic descriptor is a conceptual density-functional theory index defined at atomic site \(k\) as the difference between the local electrophilic and nucleophilic philicities,

\[
\Delta W_k = W_k^{+}-W_k^{-}.
\]

Here, \(W_k^{+}=\omega f_k^{+}\) measures the propensity of site \(k\) to accept electron density, whereas \(W_k^{-}=\omega f_k^{-}\) measures its propensity to donate electron density; \(\omega\) is the global electrophilicity index and \(f_k^{+}\) and \(f_k^{-}\) are the corresponding condensed Fukui functions. Accordingly, positive values of \(\Delta W_k\) identify locally electrophilic centers susceptible to nucleophilic attack, while negative values identify locally nucleophilic centers favored for electrophilic attack. The magnitude reflects the strength of the local preference, enabling comparison of reactive sites within a molecule and, when calculated consistently, across related reactants. The descriptor is therefore useful for predicting chemoselectivity, regioselectivity, site selectivity, and the behavior of ambiphilic or polar reaction partners. It also provides a compact connection between local philicity and the dual descriptor: because \(\Delta W_k=\omega(f_k^{+}-f_k^{-})\), the multiphilic descriptor may be viewed as the dual descriptor scaled by global electrophilicity. It thus retains the dual descriptor’s sign-based discrimination between electrophilic and nucleophilic regions while incorporating the overall electrophilic character of the molecular system.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: How can conceptual DFT combine nucleophilic and electrophilic condensed philicity functions into a single descriptor? Include relevant literature references, reaction-path analysis, predictive testing, and an associated nucleophilicity-excess measure.
counterfactuals.output:
Conceptual DFT can combine the electrophilic and nucleophilic condensed philicities through a **multiphilic—or dual-philicity—descriptor**.

## Definition

The global electrophilicity index is

\[
\omega=\frac{\mu^2}{2\eta},
\qquad
\mu \simeq-\frac{I+A}{2},
\qquad
\eta\simeq I-A ,
\]

where \(I\) and \(A\) are the vertical ionization energy and electron affinity. The condensed Fukui functions at atom \(k\), using electron populations \(Q_k\), are

\[
f_k^+=Q_k(N+1)-Q_k(N)
\]

for susceptibility toward nucleophilic attack, and

\[
f_k^-=Q_k(N)-Q_k(N-1)
\]

for susceptibility toward electrophilic attack. The corresponding condensed philicities are

\[
\omega_k^+=\omega f_k^+,\qquad
\omega_k^-=\omega f_k^- .
\]

They are combined as

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega_k
      =\omega_k^+-\omega_k^-
      =\omega\left(f_k^+-f_k^-\right)}
\]

This is the condensed **multiphilic descriptor**. It is the electrophilicity-scaled version of the dual descriptor,

\[
\Delta f_k=f_k^+-f_k^-.
\]

With this sign convention:

- \(\Delta\omega_k>0\): atom \(k\) is predominantly **electrophilic**, hence favored for nucleophilic attack;
- \(\Delta\omega_k<0\): atom \(k\) is predominantly **nucleophilic**, hence favored for electrophilic attack;
- \(\Delta\omega_k\approx0\): balanced or weakly ambiphilic behavior.

Some papers define the subtraction in the reverse order, so the equation—not merely the sign label—should always be reported. If atomic charges rather than electron populations are used, the finite-difference signs must likewise be adjusted.

## Nucleophilicity excess

The complementary **nucleophilicity-excess** quantity is

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega_k^{\mathrm{Nu}}
      =\omega_k^- - \omega_k^+
      =-\Delta\omega_k}
\]

so that a positive value directly denotes excess nucleophilic over electrophilic character. For a fragment or functional group \(G\),

\[
\Delta\omega_G^{\mathrm{Nu}}
   =\sum_{k\in G}\left(\omega_k^--\omega_k^+\right).
\]

This fragment sum is often more robust than a single-atom value when reactivity is delocalized. Because the global \(\omega\) is common to all atoms at a fixed geometry, \(\Delta\omega_k\) and \(\Delta f_k\) give the same within-molecule ranking; the philicity form becomes more useful when comparing systems or geometries with different global electrophilicities.

## Reaction-path analysis

Rather than evaluating the descriptor only at isolated reactants, it can be followed along an intrinsic reaction coordinate \(s\):

\[
\Delta\omega_k(s)
 =\omega(s)\left[f_k^+(s)-f_k^-(s)\right].
\]

A useful protocol is:

1. Optimize reactants, transition states, intermediates, and products consistently.
2. Trace the IRC in both directions from each transition state.
3. At selected IRC geometries, calculate the \(N\), \(N+1\), and \(N-1\) states at the neutral geometry—preferably with vertical \(\Delta\)SCF energies and a stable population scheme.
4. Plot \(\omega_k^+(s)\), \(\omega_k^-(s)\), \(\Delta\omega_k(s)\), and selected fragment sums.
5. Compare extrema or sign changes with bond formation, bond cleavage, charge transfer, and the transition-state position.

The preferred reacting pair should normally show complementary behavior: the nucleophilic atom has negative \(\Delta\omega_k\), or positive nucleophilicity excess, while the electrophilic partner has positive \(\Delta\omega_k\). Along the path, decreasing contrast often accompanies bond formation and electronic equalization. Sign changes can reveal polarity inversion, ambiphilic intermediates, or a switch in the dominant reaction center. Because unrestricted \(N\pm1\) calculations may suffer from spin contamination or state switching, orbital-based or fractional-electron Fukui functions provide useful checks.

## Predictive testing

A meaningful test should be prospective or cross-validated rather than based only on selected successful examples. For a set of competing sites or reaction channels:

- predict the attacked electrophilic site from the largest positive \(\Delta\omega_k\);
- predict the attacking nucleophilic site from the most negative \(\Delta\omega_k\), equivalently the largest positive \(\Delta\omega_k^{\mathrm{Nu}}\);
- for competing bond-forming pairs \(i,j\), test a simple complementarity score such as

\[
S_{ij}=\omega_i^-\,\omega_j^+
\]

or compare the corresponding fragment quantities;
- evaluate top-1 regioselectivity accuracy, rank correlation with experimental product ratios or calculated activation barriers, and sensitivity to functional, basis set, solvation model, and population analysis.

Testing should include regioisomeric electrophilic and nucleophilic additions, substitutions, and polar cycloadditions. It is important to compare against the separate \(f_k^\pm\), \(\omega_k^\pm\), electrostatic potential, and frontier-orbital coefficients. The combined descriptor is most informative for polarity and site discrimination; steric effects, conformational accessibility, solvent organization, and activation strain can override the electronic ranking.

## Relevant literature

Foundational and closely related sources include:

- R. G. Parr and W. Yang, “Density Functional Approach to the Frontier-Electron Theory of Chemical Reactivity,” **J. Am. Chem. Soc.** 1984, *106*, 4049–4050 — Fukui functions in conceptual DFT.
- R. G. Parr, L. von Szentpály, and S. Liu, “Electrophilicity Index,” **J. Am. Chem. Soc.** 1999, *121*, 1922–1924 — definition of the global electrophilicity \(\omega\).
- P. K. Chattaraj, U. Sarkar, and D. R. Roy, “Electrophilicity Index,” **Chem. Rev.** 2006, *106*, 2065–2091 — review of global and local electrophilicity/philicity concepts.
- C. Morell, A. Grand, and A. Toro-Labbé, “New Dual Descriptor for Chemical Reactivity,” **J. Phys. Chem. A** 2005, *109*, 205–212 — introduction and interpretation of \(f^+-f^-\).
- C. Morell, A. Grand, and A. Toro-Labbé, **Chem. Phys. Lett.** 2006, *425*, 342–346 — dual-descriptor analysis along chemical reactions.
- P. Geerlings, F. De Proft, and W. Langenaeker, “Conceptual Density Functional Theory,” **Chem. Rev.** 2003, *103*, 1793–1874 — broad conceptual-DFT framework.
- P. K. Chattaraj, S. Giri, and S. Duley, “Update 2 of: Electrophilicity Index,” **Chem. Rev.** 2011, *111*, PR43–PR75 — later developments, including local and multiphilic reactivity descriptors.

Thus, the concise combined measure is \(\Delta\omega_k=\omega_k^+-\omega_k^-\), while \(-\Delta\omega_k\) provides a directly signed nucleophilicity-excess measure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a concise research-paper abstract about multiphilicity, local philicity functions, soft reaction pathways, reaction force profiles, and the use of nucleophilicity excess to study intra- and intermolecular reactivity in all-metal aromatic systems.
counterfactuals.output: Conceptual density functional theory descriptors were employed to investigate intra- and intermolecular reactivity in all-metal aromatic systems. Multiphilicity and local philicity functions were used to identify electrophilic and nucleophilic regions and to quantify site selectivity, while nucleophilicity excess provided a unified measure of the competing donor–acceptor character of reactive centers. Soft reaction pathways were constructed to follow the evolution of electronic structure from reactants to products, and reaction force profiles were analyzed to partition each process into structural reorganization and electronic redistribution regimes. The combined framework reveals how aromatic delocalization, charge transfer, and local philicity govern preferred reaction channels and distinguish intramolecular rearrangements from intermolecular association. These results demonstrate that integrating global and local reactivity indices with reaction-coordinate analysis offers a coherent mechanistic description of bond formation and activation in all-metal aromatic species.
